## Study objective

The study evaluates which generative processes reproduce observed transition, repetition, predictability, and longer-range structure in vocal sequences across six parrot species.

## Comparative and modelling approach

The project analyses vocal sequences from six species in the parrot family Psittaculidae. Observed summary measures are compared with simulated sequences generated by random, Markov, hidden-Markov, and renewal processes rather than assuming a single first-order Markov model.

The selected measures quantify complementary aspects of organization, including note transitions, repetition, predictability, and longer-range sequence structure.

## Results reported in the preprint

The metrics did not identify a single preferred generative model: two measures were most closely reproduced by a renewal process and two by Markov processes. Across species, several analyses nevertheless identified an elevated probability of note repetition.

The preprint therefore identifies repetition and Markov-like transition structure as complementary components of these variable sequences. Proposed relationships between repetition and individual identity, group identity, social context, or behaviour remain hypotheses requiring context-linked and receiver-response data.

## Interpretation

Parrots provide a comparative system for studying sequence organization in open-ended vocal learners. Applying the same analytical framework across species helps distinguish recurrent structural properties from patterns specific to a species, recording context, or summary metric.
